new_statements.quote: 1.3.4 Predictability of syllable division, stress, and position of vowel length within a phonological word. ... (ii) Stress : Heavy (tonic) stress is marked [ˈ] at the beginning of the syllable. Weak stress is left unmarked. A. Monosyllabic words have heavy stress. ... B. In disyllables, when the second syllable is closed and at the same time the first syllable has a vowel other than a, the second syllable is stressed. Examples. əˈsaḍ '(a lunar month)' tiˈhar 'festival' ... But ˈa.den '(a kind of tree)' ... In all the other cases the first syllable is stressed. ... C. Words ending in a sequence of the shape VCVV have the heavy stress on their antepenultimate syllable. Examples. ˈci.ḍə.i 'bird' ... All other words having three or more than three syllables have the heavy stress on their penultimate syllable. The remaining syllables are weakly stressed. Examples. muˈṭʰe.la 'hammer' ... ci.ci.yaˈva.sit '(you,pl.) are making noise'
new_statements.citation: Kaushikkar, Chitra. 1972. Descriptive Analysis of Halbi (An Indo-Aryan Language). Poona: Deccan College [typescript Ph.D. dissertation, 322 pp.]. Read as page scan from archive.org item 20240217_20240217_2321.

In disyllables, when the second syllable is closed and at the same time the first syllable has a vowel other than a, the second syllable is stressed. Examples. əˈsaḍ.. tiˈhar 'festival' koˈṭhar 'sto…
new_statements.rule_in_words: HALBI (the language Glottolog says Mirgan is near-identical to): word stress is non-contrastive and predictable. Monosyllables stressed. Disyllables: final stress if the final syllable is closed and the first vowel is not /a/; otherwise initial stress. Words of three or more syllables: penultimate stress, except words ending in V.CV.V (onsetless final vowel), which take antepenultimate stress. Vowel length is then derived from stress placement (1.3.4 iii).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described beyond 'The remaining syllables are weakly stressed.'
new_statements.exceptions: Only the rule-internal sub-cases (initial /a/ blocks final stress in disyllables; VCVV-final polysyllables antepenult). No lexical exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly 'within a phonological word' (section heading 1.3.4); examples are citation forms including inflected verbs (oy.laˈva.se, ci.ci.yaˈva.sit). NOTE: this is a description of Halba-caste Halbi of Narayanpur tahsil, Bastar; no description of the speech of the Mirgan/Panka themselves exists in any source I could open. The statement applies to mirg1238 only via Glottolog's identity judgement (Singh 1972:11-16, 'Panki or Mirgani is essentially Halabi').
new_statements.identity_note: mirg1238 is a Glottolog BOOKKEEPING (spurious) languoid: "Mirgan [zrg] is listed in E16.E28 as a separate Indo-Aryan Eastern zone language but a survey (Singh 1972, Survey of Halabi in Madhya Pradesh: 11-16) shows it to be near identical to Halbi [hlb]". Grierson LSI VII p. 331 (1905) lists 'Mirgani' among the so-called minor dialects of Bastar Halbi and says none is a separate dialect. Ethnologue 15 (2008 Internet Archive copy) instead calls Mirgan (Panika/Panka; Bastar CG + Koraput OR; 12,000 in 1992) 'not functionally intelligible with Halbi' on the basis of an unpublished SIL survey; SCSTRTI 2015 describes the Odisha Mirgan (=Panka, migrated from Bastar) as speaking 'corrupt Odia mixed with Chhattisgarhi'. The only stress statement available is therefore the Halbi one (halb1244), which is ALREADY in the catalog from the same source (Kaushikkar 1972, data from Halba speakers of Chhotedongar, Narayanpur tahsil, Bastar - not from Panka/Mirgan speakers). Adding mirg1238 as its own catalog unit would double-count one entity; if the catalog wants a row for zrg it should be a pointer to halb1244.

sources.locator: Section 1.3.4 (ii) 'Stress', pp. 12-14 (archive.org leaves n23-n25); fieldwork basis stated in Introduction p. 12 of front matter (leaf n10): Halba village Chhotedongar, Narayanpur tahsil, Bastar, 1969-71.
sources.note: Sec. 1.3.4(ii), pp. 12-14: stress predictable within the phonological word - monosyllables heavy; disyllables stress 2nd syllable if it is closed and 1st vowel is not a, otherwise 1st syllable; words ending in VCVV antepenult; all other 3+-syllable words penult; other syllables weak. Data are Halba-caste Halbi of Chhotedongar (Narayanpur tahsil, Bastar), not Mirgan/Panka speech.
